annotations.text:
Direction D, executed modern — Plus Jakarta Sans, near-black ink on a cool off-white, one vivid teal, 22px cards on soft shadow.

Working controls, not pictures:
• Translator — the text ⇄ Morse toggle flips; tapping a letter chip selects it
• Speech — the mic cycles idle → listening → result, and the EN/PT switch changes the recognised copy
• Tap decode — press DURATION is measured for real. Tap for a dot, hold for a dash; 3 units of silence closes the letter, 7 closes the word. The cut-off stepper retunes it live.
• Settings — the threshold slider, speed and toggles all work
• Permission gates — the four states switch from the row at the bottom
• Translator · playing — the speaker button really plays: chips light letter by letter on ITU timing (dot 1, dash 3, gaps 1/3/7) and the speed chip retunes it live

App name is still open; "Morse" is a placeholder wordmark.
Settings, Learn and Tips scroll on a real phone. They are drawn here at full content height so the whole page can be reviewed at once — not as 844pt screens.

TABLET — 1180×820 landscape

One rule, two consequences:
• The bottom tab bar becomes a left rail. Same four destinations, same icons, settings drops to the bottom of the rail.
• Anything the phone stacks vertically splits into panes. Translator becomes input | output side by side; Learn puts the reading matter beside the reference grid, which reflows from 4 columns to 6.

Nothing here is a new screen — each is the phone layout above a width breakpoint, which is why it is worth settling now rather than retrofitting.

THREE UI LANGUAGES — English, Português (Brasil), Español

The whole interface translates, not just the input. These two are the same artboard as the English Translator with only the strings swapped, so any layout difference is purely string length.

What that surfaced: the Morse card's header row put its label and its hint on one line with no shrink protection. It fit in English at 390pt and would have collided at 360pt in Portuguese. Both now shrink and wrap; every phone frame was re-checked at 360pt.

Accented letters — decided: Ç (-.-..), É (..-..) and Ñ (--.--) have real ITU codes and are supported; every other diacritic is sent as its base letter. Ñ and Ç are distinct letters, not decoration (año ≠ ano), and the rest have no standard code. All three are in the Learn alphabet with the rule stated underneath.

OUTPUTS — one message, several channels

Decided 2026-09-03. There is ONE run of the message. The four cells choose which ways it goes out, and they are live: turn Light on mid-message and the torch joins the sound already in progress, in step. Turning them all off leaves Send it with nothing to do.

That replaces the old row, where Flash it was a separate primary action that merely switched the torch on and left it on. Flash it is now the Light channel; the primary button runs the message.

Why not one play button per output: pressing a second one mid-message would start that output from the beginning while the first is halfway through — the same message transmitted twice, out of step, with one progress bar unable to say which it was tracking.

Progress still reads twice: the chips carry played / sounding / pending, the thin track carries the exact position. Both describe the one run, whichever channels are carrying it.

Sound defaults ON, Light defaults OFF — decided 2026-09-03. Switching Light on is what raises the camera permission, and a new user's first press should not open a system dialog before they have heard anything. With every channel off the button is disabled rather than running a progress bar over silence. All four channels are built. Vibration works differently by platform and cannot be made to match: Android reproduces the marks by duration, while iOS cannot vary a vibration's length at all, so it fires a pulse at each mark's START with intensity carrying dot from dash — the rhythm is exact, the durations are not.



Propagated 2026-09-03 to Main, both locale variants and the tablet. The cells are static there — Playing is the artboard that demonstrates toggling.

FIRST RUN — three slides

Exists because Light starts off. Without it the torch is a feature nobody finds, and the strip looks like decoration.

The illustrations are the app's own components, not invented artwork: real letter chips, the real channel strip, the real Signal button. What the carousel promises is exactly what the next screen shows.

Slide 2 is the one that had to exist. It says plainly which channels are on, why Light is not, and that any of them can be changed at any time — including mid-message.

Skip jumps to the last slide rather than dismissing outright, so the Start button is always the way out. One way in, one way out.

WHEN IT SHOWS — decided 2026-09-03. Gated on a stored version number, not a seen/unseen flag, so it can be shown again after an update that adds something worth explaining. The version is configurable rather than hard-wired.

For now it is set to show ONCE: the version stays put, so nobody sees it twice. Revisit when every screen exists — Screen and Vibrate are drawn in the strip but not built, and slide 2 has to be rewritten when they land.

SCREEN — the flicker surface (a disc)

While Screen is on and a message runs, the Morse chips give way to a disc that flips between near-black and white on the signal. The chips are a reading aid; at that moment the square IS the message.

⚠️ THE SIZE IS A SAFETY CONSTRAINT, not a layout preference. Morse flashes at 4.2Hz at 10 WPM and 6.3Hz at 15 — both far past WCAG 2.3.1's limit of three flashes per second. The only compliant route left is keeping the flashing area under 25% of the visual field. A 240pt disc is 13.7% of a 390x844 screen — a circle covers only pi/4 of its bounding box, so the shape buys headroom the square did not have.

So full-screen is NOT available, however much more legible it would be across a room. If it ever gets bigger, it needs a photosensitivity warning ahead of it and probably a setting.

It is also sized against the space it is given rather than fixed, after a fixed 240 overflowed the card and was clipped. The artboard flips by button rather than animating, for the same reason — a design canvas is not the place to strobe at 6Hz.

Keeping the screen awake: done. The app holds it for the length of a run and lets it go at the end, so a long message no longer hits auto-lock part-way through.

WHAT IS BUILT — reconciled 2026-09-04

These artboards now describe the app as it actually is. Three things were drawn here and never built, and have been taken out rather than left standing as promises:

• Speech had a language switcher. The screen listens in the interface language and offers no second choice; changing language is the Language screen's job. Worth revisiting if a bilingual user asks.
• Speech had a Flash it button and a re-record button. Flash it was a leftover of the Translator action row that no longer exists anywhere, and tapping the mic again already re-records.
• Tap gained a Clear action the artboard did not have.

One thing went the other way: the Tap key had drifted in CODE into a full-width rounded rectangle. The artboard had settled it as a 186pt disc with a ring, and the code now matches the design rather than the design being rewritten around the drift.

Still drawn as the finished app rather than as today's build:
• The Learn tab is greyed and inert in the running app because that screen does not exist yet. The artboards show it normal on purpose — the design is the finished thing, and encoding a build-order artefact into it would be wrong the week Learn lands.
• The Translator's "no code for" notice only appears when unencodable characters are typed, so it is not in the idle artboard.

Not built at all yet: Settings, Learn, Tips, Permissions, Language, and both tablet layouts.
